input.question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?
input.ground_truth: Chess is a unique game, in that each piece has only certain moves that can be performed at any time, and thus one can predict which moves will be done many turns in advance, and each move to counter them. There is really no "randomness" in chance. This allows a computer to be programmed to constantly monitor the positions of each piece on the board, and do exactly that, think 10+ turns ahead and figure out each counterplay to each possible movement of each piece on the board, your own and your opponents. & #x200B; It's very close to what a grandmaster in chess does, however, a computer is not subject to stress or other interferences.

Question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a robot friend who loves to play chess with you. At first, the robot doesn’t know how to play at all. But every time you play, the robot watches what you do and remembers.

Later, people teach the robot lots and lots of chess games—millions! They show the robot how good players move their pieces and what tricks they use. The robot doesn’t sleep; it keeps practicing all the time, playing millions of games against itself in its brain.

Also, the robot has a super-fast brain (called a computer) that can think about many moves at once. It can try out “what if I move this piece here?” and “what if my friend moves that piece there?” really, really fast.

So, after practicing a lot and thinking super fast, the robot gets really good at chess—sometimes even better than people! That’s how computers got so smart at playing chess.
